newsitem.title: USA: World oil demand to rise 2.1 percent in 1997-EIA.
newsitem.headline: World oil demand to rise 2.1 percent in 1997-EIA.

text.p: World oil demand in 1997 should continue to rise to record levels, and should average 73.4 million barrels per day, up 2.1 percent from 1996, the Energy Information Administration said Friday.
By 1998, world energy demand should average 75.2 million barrels per day, the EIA said in its short-term outlook.

"All indicators point toward continued annual increments of 1.5 million barrels per day worldwide in 1997 and 1.8 million barrels per day in 1998, or an annual average growth of 2.3 percent compared with the 1.3 percent average growth seen between 1991 and 1995," the EIA said.
Oil demand in industrialized countries should rise by about 1 percent in 1997 to 41.7 million bpd in 1997, and by 1.4 percent in 1998 to 42.3 million bpd.
The United States' demand should increase by 1.1 percent to 18.4 million bpd in 1997, and by 1.6 percent to 18.7 million bpd in 1998.
U.S. oil demand growth represents about 30 percent of OECD growth in 1997, but over half of the demand growth in 1998, the EIA said.
In developing countries, oil demand was seen rising 3.6 percent in 1997 to 31.7 million bpd, and by 3.5 percent in 1998 to 32.8 million bpd.
Demand in the former Soviet Union is projected to increase slightly in 1997 and 1998 following years of major declines, up from 4.7 milion bpd in 1996 to 4.8 million bpd in both 1997 and 1998.

The EIA said the additional 600,000 bpd to come on the world market from the United Nation's oil-for-food agreement with Iraq, along with additional non-OPEC output, should provide enough oil so that production from OPEC will increase just slightly to cover the increased demand.
Despite the adequate supplies, OPEC countries including Venezuela and Nigeria were expected to increase production through 1998.
